text:
A: Hiya! Hi, can you hear me? I'm Holly.
B: Hi, yeah, I can hear you. I'm Lauren. Sorry, the light's a bit rubbish in here.
A: No, you're fine! Mine's all blue from the screen anyway. Where are you based?
B: Basingstoke. It's, erm, sort of near Reading. Not very exciting.
A: Ah, don't say that! I'm in Birmingham, so I can't judge anyone. Was that a cat in your photo? On the cushion?
B: Yeah, that's Biscuit. He's ginger and he's quite old. He actually came into the practice I work at to be put to sleep, and then he just never was. He came home with me instead.
A: Oh my god, stop, that's the best story. So you work at a vet's?
B: Yeah, I'm a vet nurse. Registered. It's a small practice, just cats and dogs and the odd rabbit.
A: That's amazing. I've got a greyhound, Pickle, she's on the settee behind me, you can sort of see her tail. She's a rescue too. She's terrified of rain, like properly refuses to go out, she just plants her feet at the door and looks at me like I've betrayed her.
B: Greyhounds are lovely. They're such big babies. We get them in and they shake on the table and you just want to wrap them in a blanket. Erm, they're really sensitive to anaesthetic as well, actually, because they've got hardly any body fat, so we have to be really careful with them.
A: Wait, really? I didn't know that.
B: Yeah, they sort of take longer to come round. I do a lot of the anaesthetic monitoring, so I'm always a bit on edge with sighthounds. Sorry, that's probably more than you wanted to know.
A: No, that's genuinely useful! Pickle's having a dental next month, so I'm going to be that owner asking about her body fat now. What made you go into it?
B: I've always just liked animals more than people, I think. Not in a horrible way. I did an apprenticeship after school, three years, college one day a week and the rest on the job. So I didn't do uni or anything.
A: Honestly that sounds way more useful than what I'm doing. I'm doing a PhD in geography, which mostly means I take photos of derelict warehouses and then panic about chapters.
B: That sounds really clever though.
A: It sounds clever. It's sort of, kind of, you know, half vibes. I had a call just before this with a lady who cleans a school at night, and she said empty classrooms with the chairs up on the tables are like my warehouses, and I've basically decided that's my whole conference paper now.
B: That's quite a nice way of putting it, actually.
A: Isn't it? Anyway, what do you do when you're not working? Do you get any time off?
B: Not loads. I'm on lates this week so I'm a bit shattered. I read a lot. And I do cross-stitch, mostly animals. The one behind me is a cat.
A: Oh, I saw that! I thought you'd bought it. That's so neat. I paint, but badly. My canvases look like a toddler's had a go after a few drinks.
B: I'm sure they don't.
A: No, they do, and I've made peace with it. Do you do gigs or anything, or are you more of a stay-in person?
B: Stay-in, mostly. Crowds aren't really my thing. I'll listen to Phoebe Bridgers on a walk on my own, if that makes sense?
A: No, that totally makes sense. I went to a gig in Digbeth last weekend and someone spilled a whole pint down my back, so honestly you was right all along.
B: That's sort of exactly why I don't go.
A: Ha! Fair enough. So what's the worst bit about the job, if that's not too heavy?
B: Erm, probably the euthanasias. You'd think you'd get used to it but I don't, really. I still cry in the car sometimes.
